prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength open a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. I have tried to test it against the chair's questions and not simply rest on the fact that seven of eight files agree. First, distinctness. The 2005 comb prize gave us the ability to count optical cycles, and the 2012 prize concerned the control of single quantum systems, with the ion clock as one application. The magic-wavelength lattice is neither of these. It is a new way of holding thousands of neutral atoms so that Doppler, recoil and light shifts are all cancelled at once, which turns a statistical advantage into an accuracy advantage. That is why uncertainty fell by orders of magnitude to about 1e-18, and why the result has been reproduced at RIKEN, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere. The citation should therefore name the lattice, not clocks in general. Second, the argument is about capability and not about a fundamental discovery. The constancy-of-constants tests have so far given null results and I will not ask the committee to pretend otherwise. What nature has been asked is a sharper question than before, with gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, and the answer is a measurement regime that did not exist. Third, two names. Katori had the concept and the first strontium lattice clock; Ye took the systematic uncertainty to the frontier and built the many-body Fermi-degenerate clock. No colleague has shown a specific decisive contribution by a third person that is separable from these two. Fourth, I do not think the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second. The performance is already measured and reproduced, and the redefinition will follow from the prize-worthy work, not be a precondition of it.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 and 2012 remains the strongest reservation and I cannot argue it away completely. A reader who sees the lattice clock as an extension of precision spectroscopy will see a continuation. The citation wording can reduce that risk but cannot remove it. The redefinition of the SI second has not happened, so part of the payoff is still prospective. The credit has a hard boundary, since Lemonde, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow and Oates and the SYRTE group are outside it, and I accept that a two-name prize leaves some real contributors unnamed. Finally, this is a measurement achievement and not a new phase of matter or a new window on the universe, which means the surprise to the broader scientific community is smaller than for B010 or B032. I have not found a reading of those candidates that overcomes their own immaturity or attribution problems this year, but I do not claim they are weaker science.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B010 first because the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction preceded the 2018 experiments, and in his case_against he concedes that a maturity-first reading would put B004 ahead and that atomic-physics colleagues must decide whether clocks are distinct from earlier prizes.
responses.response: He asks atomic-physics colleagues to settle the distinctness question, and I will try to state it in terms a condensed-matter theorist can test. Ask what each earlier prize would not have produced without the lattice. A comb alone gives a ruler for optical frequencies, and a single trapped ion gives a good but one-particle reference, with the signal-to-noise limit that implies. The magic-wavelength lattice is what allows many atoms to be probed with the perturbation cancelled, so it is what makes 1e-18 reachable in a reasonable averaging time. That is a theoretical idea, tested by experiment, which I think is exactly the kind of prediction-then-confirmation structure he values in B010. I continue to share his respect for the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction, but I do not move B010 up. The pairing mechanism is open, the field is about eight years old, and Cao is omitted from the trio. Those are reasons to wait one cycle, and I would support B010 in a later year if the attribution can be handled.

responses.point: Olsson cannot settle whether Katori's magic-wavelength proposal or the first operational lattice clock marks the original contribution, and says that if credit cannot be apportioned to two people without distorting the record, B010 is the better-structured alternative.
responses.response: I think the record does answer this, and in favour of two names. The idea and its first realisation both belong to Katori, who proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first strontium lattice clock, so the proposal-versus-demonstration question does not separate him from his own work. What follows is Ye's contribution, which is the accuracy and stability records and the many-body clock, and that is a distinct step with its own physics. So the citation can honestly say invention and realisation for the first and, through the 1e-18 performance, for the second. I would resist the idea that B010 is better structured on attribution. Cao's omission from a three-name set is a bigger distortion of the record than anything I can find in the B004 pair, and Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto add a further layer. I therefore keep B004 as the better-structured case, while agreeing with her that if the second is redefined it could sharpen the wording.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B004 is largely a refinement of precision spectroscopy and that its conceptual surprise is smaller than a new phase or a new window, though he says the systematic shifts are controlled by theory that matches experiment.
responses.response: I accept his description of the weakness and I want to answer it on his own terms, because he is the member who prefers simple, universal mechanisms. The lattice clock is not simple because it is a refinement; it is simple because one idea, cancelling the differential light shift at a magic wavelength, replaces a whole list of limitations. The surprise is that a trap, which usually perturbs the very transition you want to measure, can be made not to. The fact he notes, that blackbody, higher-order lattice and collision shifts are all understood quantitatively, is why this is physics and not engineering. I would still ask him not to treat B007 as lost. His point about the 2016 topological-defect overlap is fair, and I would not want to see it come back as a standalone prize before that is resolved, but I do not read his move to B004 as a retreat from conceptual merit.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether a two-part prize pairing the clock with a quantum-technology topic such as circuit QED would be worth the loss of credit coherence, and has B034 and B036 as alternatives.
responses.response: I would not add a second part this year. The chair asked who would present the second case and with what laureates, and nobody has. B034 has two different trios in the opening proposals (Johansson's with Blais, Kroll's with Girvin), and Johansson has flagged a possible conflict. In addition, the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum behaviour in superconducting circuits makes me want to avoid appearing to honour the same family of devices twice in a row. B036 atom interferometry is a respectable case, but it is a different capability with its own history, and combining it with the clock would give a two-topic prize whose citation would have to be cut down to be coherent. Kroll's own point that the single topic keeps the credit coherent is, I think, the right criterion and it decides the matter for me.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, asks whether a second part such as B032 or B036 should be added and raises Ye's appearance in other candidacies; he also ranked IceCube second.
responses.response: I ranked B032 second and I still regard it as a serious candidate, but the reasons I gave in round 1 still hold. The diffuse flux is firm, whereas the individual source associations are modest and KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are only partly independent. Attribution to two names also means leaving out a collaboration of hundreds, which is unavoidable but should be settled when the picture has matured, not squeezed in as a second part now. On Ye, I do not see that his name appearing in other candidacies bears on this configuration. If the committee chooses B004, he is credited on the merits of the lattice-clock work, and any other candidacy would be a separate matter in a different year. I would, however, record the observation so nobody later says it was overlooked.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes, which depends partly on citation wording.
Whether a prize that is justified by capability, with constancy-of-constants tests still giving null results, will be read as a prize for an instrument and not for a discovery.
Whether the exclusion of Lemonde, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow, Oates and the SYRTE group is defensible, since nobody has yet shown a third separable contribution that would justify a third seat.
Whether the redefinition of the SI second, if it occurs soon, would change the timing or the wording of the citation.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has appeared for B004 since round 1, and I have no tie to Katori or Ye. My ties to David Gross, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string-theory group are unrelated to any shortlisted candidate. I repeat that my opening first choice, B045 on baryon acoustic oscillations, is in my own cosmology field, and I treat that as a bias to discount, not as a reason to keep pressing it. I also note, as an observation and not a recusal matter, that I have no stake in B034 or B043, where Johansson has declared a possible conflict.
